feedback: If a prediction is made without reference to the data, ask: 'Show me on your results why you predicted that distance' and require the prediction to sit on the trend.
If a near miss is treated as failure, introduce repeat readings and a 'close enough / within range' judgement — predictions from patterns are trend-based, not exact.
If more than one thing is changed between trials (e.g. moving the start point or adding a push), rebuild the test so only ramp height changes: same release point, no push.
If only one reading is taken per height, scaffold a second and third reading and compare, so noise is not mistaken for pattern.

If the changed condition and the measured quantity are muddled in recording, prompt the child to label one column 'ramp height' (what we change) and another 'distance rolled' (what we measure), so the pattern can be read cleanly.
When a self-discovered trend correctly foretells a motion never measured, name that moment explicitly: the data predicted the result.
activities.intendedInsight: A pattern found across many readings can be used to make and justify a prediction about an untested, related case; a prediction grounded in your own data is an evidence-based inference, not a guess.
learnerActions: Start from a 'big question': 'Does a steeper ramp make the car roll further?'
Set up real apparatus — a ramp you can prop at different heights, a toy car, a metre rule, and (optionally) a stopwatch.
Release the car from the SAME start point each time, raising the ramp in steps, and measure the distance it rolls for each height.

Take repeat readings (at least two or three) at each height, and record all readings systematically in a table that keeps the changed condition (ramp height) and the measured quantity (distance rolled) in separate labelled columns.
Plot the results on a graph (bar, line, or scatter as appropriate) so the trend across readings becomes visible.
Use 'what do you notice?' to state the relationship in your own words (e.g. 'for the heights we tried, the steeper the ramp, the further it rolls').

PREDICT, THEN TEST: for a ramp height you have NOT tried, use the pattern to predict the roll distance (best between your measured heights; if beyond them, only a little and with more caution), mark it, then run that height and compare the car's actual stop to your prediction.
Judge success by how close the actual distance is to the predicted trend, not by an exact hit, and raise a new 'big question' the enquiry suggests.
activities.title: Hands-on ramp-and-car pattern investigation
